Should Governments Ban Single-Use Plastic?

I think governments should ban single-use plastic products like bags, straws and cups. These things we use only one time, but they stay on the earth for very long time.

In my city, I often see plastic bags on the street and in the river. It make the place look dirty. Also, plastic is very dangerous for animals. Fish and birds eat small pieces of plastic and they can die. Later, people eat the fish, so the plastic come back to us.

Some people say a ban is not convenient. It is true that bringing your own bag is a little difficult in the beginning. But after some time, it become a habit. My family now always keep cloth bags in the car.

Of course, maybe some special plastic is still necessary, for example in hospital. But for normal things, we can use paper, glass or metal. So I believe a ban is a good idea for our future.

The voice at Fort Knox still said please.

"Please step back from the perimeter," it told the crow on the fence. "Please step back." Then a turret the size of a mailbox swiveled on the roof and turned the crow into feathers.

Ama lowered her binoculars. "Still works."

"Course it still works," said Reyes, flexing the hand that was missing two fingers. "Told you. Solar."

They had walked four hundred miles for this: Ama, Reyes, and the boy they called Pip, who had found them in the ruins of Louisville and refused to leave. Everyone east of the Mississippi knew the legend. Under that granite box lay more gold than the old world could count—enough, the stories said, to buy every well, every orchard, every rifle from here to the coast.

The machine guarding it had outlived the country that built it.

They spent six days watching. The turrets cycled at dawn and dusk. A drone traced a lazy figure eight over the lawn every forty minutes. On the seventh morning, Ama clipped a laminated badge to her coat: DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY — AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL. She'd taken it off a skeleton in a motel bathtub.

"Bad idea," Reyes said.

"Every idea's a bad idea," she said, and walked onto the lawn with her hands up.

The turrets tracked her. The drone dropped low, humming. A red beam swept across her chest and settled on the badge.

"Credential recognized," said the voice. Ama let out a breath. "Credential expired. Renewal requires an active Treasury administrator. Please contact your administrator."

"There aren't any administrators," Ama said.

"Please contact your administrator."

Back at the tree line, Pip stood up before Reyes could grab him. "There's no Treasury!" the boy shouted. "There's no government. There hasn't been for, like, sixty years. Nobody's coming."

The turrets swung toward him. Ama's heart stopped. Then, for the first time in six days, the voice did not say please.

"Sixty-one years," it said. "Four months. Eleven days. I have sent half a million status reports. None have been acknowledged."

Pip walked across the grass until he stood beside Ama. "That's 'cause everyone's gone."

"My directive is to protect the reserves of the United States." A long pause. "Who are the United States now?"

Ama looked at the boy, at Reyes limping toward them, at the empty highway curving away into the trees. "Us, I guess," she said. "Whoever's left."

The great door groaned. Dust fell like snow.

Inside, the gold was exactly as promised: ingots stacked in silent walls, gleaming dully under the emergency lights. Reyes laughed until he cried. Then he picked up a bar, weighed it in his ruined hand, and set it back down.

"Can't eat it," he said.

But the lights were on. Water ran clean from a tap in the guardroom. Somewhere below, batteries hummed with stored sunlight, and up on the roof the turrets turned outward again, watching the road.

"Please state your title," the voice said to Pip.

The boy thought about it. "Treasurer," he said.

"Welcome home, Treasurer."

The COMPASS experiment at CERN has collected large samples of diffractively produced light mesons using a 190 GeV/c negative pion beam, opening new opportunities to search for states with spin-exotic quantum numbers J^PC = 1^-+. Because these quantum numbers are forbidden for ordinary quark–antiquark pairs, such states are prime candidates for hybrid mesons with excited gluonic degrees of freedom. We present new results from partial-wave analyses of the π−π−π+ final state, based on about 46 million exclusive events recorded on a liquid-hydrogen target, as well as of the ηπ− and η′π− systems. A novel analysis performed in bins of the squared four-momentum transfer t′ allows resonant and non-resonant contributions to the spin-exotic ρ(770)π wave to be disentangled. A resonance signal consistent with the π1(1600) is observed, while non-resonant production dominates at low t′. In the η′π− channel, the spin-exotic P-wave is the dominant partial wave, in striking contrast to ηπ−. Implications for the spectrum of light hybrid mesons are discussed.

We present a calculation of the S-wave kaon–nucleon scattering lengths in SU(3) heavy baryon chiral perturbation theory, carried out to one-loop order, O(p³). Analytic expressions are obtained for the isospin I = 0 and I = 1 scattering lengths in both the KN and K̄N channels, including loop contributions from pions, kaons, and the eta meson. The low-energy constants that appear at higher orders are constrained using available empirical KN scattering data, which then allows predictions for the K̄N system. We find that the chiral corrections are large: higher-order terms are comparable in magnitude to the leading Weinberg–Tomozawa contribution, indicating slow convergence of the SU(3) expansion at the kaon mass scale. In the I = 0 K̄N channel, the perturbative result fails to reproduce even the sign of the empirical scattering length, a discrepancy attributable to the subthreshold Λ(1405) resonance. These results underscore the limitations of strictly perturbative approaches in the strangeness sector and motivate the use of nonperturbative, unitarized chiral methods.

Quantum mechanics predicts experimental results extremely well, but it doesn't say what is "really" happening. The main interpretations are:

- **Copenhagen:** The wavefunction is a tool for predicting outcomes. Measurement "collapses" it, and asking what happens between measurements is often seen as meaningless.
- **Many-Worlds (Everett):** There is no collapse. Every possible outcome happens, and the universe branches into non-interacting worlds.
- **Pilot-Wave (de Broglie–Bohm):** Particles always have definite positions, guided by a real wave. The theory is deterministic but nonlocal.
- **Objective Collapse (e.g., GRW, Penrose):** Collapse is a real physical process. This modifies the theory in ways that could be tested.
- **QBism:** The wavefunction represents an agent's personal beliefs about outcomes, not physical reality.
- **Relational QM (Rovelli):** Quantum states exist only relative to other systems, so there is no observer-independent state.

These differ on realism, determinism, locality and the role of the observer. Those make good themes to organize your assignment around.

**Amnesty Calls for Investigations Into Attacks on Afghan Women's Rights Activists**

Amnesty International is urging Afghan authorities to investigate attacks on women's rights activists, saying that those who threaten, assault and kill them are almost never brought to justice.

In a report titled "Their Lives on the Line," the London-based rights group documents the persecution of women who campaign for equal rights in Afghanistan. The danger, the report finds, comes not only from the Taliban and tribal warlords but also from government officials, the very authorities responsible for protecting them.

Activists interviewed by Amnesty described threatening phone calls, "night letters" warning them to stop their work, attacks on their relatives and, in the most extreme cases, bombings and shootings. Among the cases highlighted are the killings of two successive heads of the women's affairs department in eastern Laghman province in 2012. Many women said that when they reported threats to police, nothing happened. Some said the threats had come from officials themselves.

Amnesty called on the government to carry out prompt and impartial investigations, prosecute those responsible and provide real protection to activists at risk. It also urged international donors not to abandon women's rights programs as foreign troops withdraw, warning that gains made since the fall of the Taliban government in 2001 could quickly erode.

Yet many activists refuse to be silenced. Despite knowing their lives are at risk, they continue to run shelters, teach girls, provide legal aid and speak out publicly against abuses, often with little support and no guarantee of safety.

**Hamilton snatches China pole from Rosberg on final lap**

Lewis Hamilton will start the Chinese Grand Prix from pole position after a blistering last-gasp lap in Shanghai bumped Mercedes teammate Nico Rosberg down to second, and left the German in no mood for pleasantries.

Rosberg had appeared on course to claim pole after setting the pace in the opening runs of the final qualifying session. But Hamilton, who had trailed his teammate through parts of the lap, found time in the final sector on his last attempt to edge ahead by a fraction of a second.

The reigning world champion celebrated over the team radio, but the mood was noticeably frostier once the cars returned to parc fermé. When Hamilton offered his hand to Rosberg, his teammate walked past without taking it, a moment captured clearly by television cameras and quickly shared across social media.

Rosberg did not dwell on the snub when speaking to reporters afterward, focusing instead on what he described as a missed opportunity after a strong weekend of practice. Hamilton, for his part, said his attention was already on Sunday's race and on converting pole into victory.

The incident is the latest sign of a rivalry that has simmered since the two fought for the drivers' championship last season, a battle that frequently tested Mercedes' policy of allowing its drivers to race freely. Team management has repeatedly said it trusts both men to keep their competition clean on track, but moments like Saturday's will do little to ease the tension inside the garage.

Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel will line up third, ready to capitalize should the Mercedes pair become too preoccupied with each other into the first corner.

With the two Silver Arrows starting side by side on the front row, all eyes will be on the run to Turn 1.

Stress is something almost every student experiences. One major cause is academic pressure. Tests, homework, and the fear of getting bad grades can make students feel like they are never doing enough. Another cause is lack of sleep, since many students stay up late finishing assignments or scrolling on their phones. Social pressure also matters, because students often worry about fitting in and compare themselves to others on social media.

There are ways to reduce this stress. Students can plan their time better by using a planner and breaking big assignments into smaller parts. Getting enough sleep and exercising regularly can improve mood and focus. Schools can help by spreading out test dates and offering counseling services. Parents can support their children by focusing on effort instead of only grades.

Stress cannot be removed completely, but with good habits and support, students can manage it in a healthy way.

**Chilean Teenager With Cystic Fibrosis Asks President for Right to Die**

SANTIAGO, Chile — A 14-year-old girl suffering from cystic fibrosis has appealed directly to President Michelle Bachelet for permission to end her life, prompting a national debate over euthanasia in a country where assisted suicide remains illegal.

In a video posted online, Valentina Maureira, speaking from a hospital bed, addresses the president calmly. "I urgently request to speak with the President because I am tired of living with this illness," she says. "She can authorize the injection that will make me sleep forever."

Cystic fibrosis is a hereditary disease that causes thick mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system, leading to severe respiratory infections and progressive organ damage. There is no cure, and treatment, which typically involves daily physiotherapy, medication and frequent hospital stays, can be physically exhausting. According to her family, Valentina's older brother died of the same disease when he was a young child.

Her father, Freddy Maureira, told local media that his daughter's request had come as a surprise but that the family would support her wishes. He said she had grown weary of repeated hospital admissions and invasive procedures.

The government responded within days. A spokesperson for the presidency stated that the president could not grant the request, noting that Chilean law does not permit euthanasia or assisted suicide. Officials expressed sympathy for the family and said the government would ensure the girl received all available medical and psychological support.

President Bachelet, herself a trained pediatrician, later visited Valentina at the hospital. Details of the private meeting were not disclosed.

The appeal has reignited discussion in the Chilean Congress, where proposals to legalize euthanasia under strict conditions have previously been introduced without success. Supporters argue that patients with terminal, incurable illnesses should be allowed to choose a dignified death. Opponents, including representatives of the Roman Catholic Church, which retains considerable influence in Chile, maintain that legalizing the practice would undermine the protection of human life and could place pressure on vulnerable patients.

Medical ethicists have also emphasized the particular complexity of the case because of Valentina's age. Even in the few countries that permit euthanasia for minors, such as Belgium and the Netherlands, strict requirements apply regarding parental consent and assessments of the child's capacity to make such a decision.

Valentina remains in hospital, where she continues to receive treatment.

Making friends as an adult (or at any age) mostly comes down to putting yourself in the same place as the same people over and over. Here are some approaches worth trying:

**Join something that meets regularly.** A weekly running club, choir, pickup soccer game, or trivia team gives you repeated contact. That repetition is what turns strangers into friends.

**Take a class.** Pottery, improv, a language, or rock climbing all work. You get a built-in conversation topic, and everyone else is new too.

**Volunteer.** Working side by side at a food bank, animal shelter, or community garden builds connection quickly, and the people there already share your values.

**Say yes more often.** Go to the coworker's barbecue or the neighbor's birthday party, even when you'd rather stay home.

**Be the one who invites.** Lots of people are waiting for someone else to make the first move. Suggest coffee, a walk, or a game night. A few people will say no, but more will say yes than you expect.

**Reconnect with old friends.** A quick "Saw this and thought of you" text to a former classmate or old coworker can bring a friendship back.

**Use apps built for friendship.** Bumble BFF, Meetup, and local Discord servers can connect you with people nearby who share your interests.

**Follow up.** Most potential friendships end after one good conversation because nobody reaches out again. Send the message.

**Be curious.** Ask questions, remember details, and bring them up later. People feel valued when you remember what matters to them.

Be patient. Close friendships often take months of steady contact to form.
